title: Test Game
intro: A Category 4 hurricane named Wren is forecast to make landfall near the coastal town of Port Haven in about 48 hours. The same storm looks very different depending on who you are. Choose your character to begin.

modes.label: Base Scenario
modes.description: Face the storm with the resources you have on hand — no outside help, no advance preparation.

modes.label: Community Involvement & Support
modes.description: The same storm, but your community and outside support show up to help you face it.

modes.label: Proactive Risk Resilience
modes.description: Invest in a resilience measure before the storm season, then live with the results when Wren arrives.

characters.name: Dr. Maya Chen
characters.description: You lead a regional climate and storm-surge modeling team. Emergency managers and the public look to your forecasts to decide what to do.

characters.name: Sam Rivera
characters.description: You run a 200-acre farm with a cattle herd just outside Port Haven. Everything you own is in the storm's path, and time is short.

sci_start.title: The Forecast Lands
sci_start.text:
It's 6 a.m. and the overnight model runs are in. Hurricane Wren is intensifying faster than expected. The official forecast still shows a wide landfall window — anywhere across 80 miles of coastline, including Port Haven.

Emergency managers are asking for your team's guidance. You have two days of compute and daylight to spend wisely.

choices.text: Run a high-resolution ensemble to narrow the landfall and storm-surge window before advising anyone.
Skip the deeper analysis — brief emergency managers right now with the data you already have.

sci_model.title: Into the Models
sci_model.text:
You spend the morning running a high-resolution ensemble. By noon a clear signal emerges: Wren will likely track slightly west, pushing a storm surge of 12–15 feet into the low-lying western neighborhoods of Port Haven — far worse than the public forecast suggests.

The science is solid, but acting on it means recommending a disruptive evacuation a full day before the storm.

choices.text: Recommend a mandatory evacuation of the low-lying western zones now.
Hold off one more hour — first gauge whether an upstream rain band could stack river flooding on top of the surge.

sci_compound_roll.title: Compounding Risk: The Stalled Rain Band
sci_compound_roll.text:
There's a second threat the public forecast is glossing over. A slow-moving rain band is parked over the river's upstream watershed. If it stalls, the runoff will pour downstream and meet the storm tide head-on — turning two manageable floods into one catastrophe.

The atmospheric models split on whether it stalls. It comes down to the next few hours. Roll to see how the watershed plays out.

roll.prompt: Click the die. If it lands on a 2 or a 4, the rain band stalls and the floods compound.
roll.goodText: The rain band drifts out to sea. The watershed stays within its banks — you're dealing with the surge alone, exactly as modeled.
roll.badText: The rain band stalls. Upstream rivers are already cresting, and that water is heading for the same coastline as the surge. The flood footprint just doubled.

sci_compound_clear.title: Back to the Surge
sci_compound_clear.text: With the compounding flood threat off the table, you can give emergency managers a clean, confident message about the storm surge alone. The only question left is how forcefully to push it.

choices.text: Recommend a mandatory evacuation of the western zones now.
Recommend only a voluntary evacuation to avoid panic.

sci_compound_hit.title: Two Floods at Once
sci_compound_hit.text: Your screen tells the story: river gauges upstream are spiking while the surge builds offshore. The combined flood will reach neighborhoods nobody planned to evacuate. You have minutes, not hours, to change the official response.

choices.text: Call the emergency director and demand an immediate expanded evacuation across the whole flood footprint.
Stick with the western-zone plan — a last-minute expansion could cause more chaos than the flood.

sci_compound_evac.title: Ahead of Both Floods
sci_compound_evac.text:
Your warning detonates through the chain of command. Officials expand the evacuation to the entire combined flood zone with hours to spare. It is enormous, expensive, and deeply unpopular — right up until the river and the sea arrive together and swallow streets no prior plan had ever flagged.

The water takes homes. It does not take lives. In the after-action reviews, your insistence on modeling the compounding risk — the flood nobody else was looking for — is credited with the empty, survivable streets. The hardest forecasts to make are the ones about two disasters at once.

sci_overrun.title: The Flood Nobody Planned For
sci_overrun.text:
You hold the line on the western-zone plan. Then the rivers and the surge arrive together, exactly as the gauges warned, and pour into neighborhoods that were never told to leave.

The rescues stretch into days. The compounding flood was in your data hours before it happened — you saw it, and you let the fear of a messy, last-minute evacuation talk you out of acting. That silence is the part you'll carry.

sci_brief_early.title: An Early Warning
sci_brief_early.text:
You brief the emergency management team by mid-morning. Without the high-resolution run, your confidence is low and the officials are hesitant — a needless evacuation is expensive and erodes public trust for the next storm.

"Give us something firmer," they say, "or give us a reason to move now."

choices.text: Push hard for a precautionary evacuation despite the uncertainty.
Hold off — wait for the afternoon model runs before pushing.

sci_evac.title: Ahead of the Water
sci_evac.text:
Officials issue a mandatory evacuation of the western zones the day before landfall. It's chaotic and unpopular — until Wren makes landfall exactly where your models said it would.

A 14-foot surge floods the western neighborhoods overnight. The streets are underwater, but they're empty. No lives are lost in the evacuated zones.

In the weeks that follow, your team's high-resolution surge modeling becomes the template for the whole region. Sometimes the most important science is the kind that gets people to move in time.

sci_voluntary.title: A Half-Heeded Warning
sci_voluntary.text:
A voluntary evacuation goes out. Many families leave — but plenty stay, reassured by the calmer official forecast and unwilling to abandon their homes.

When the 14-foot surge arrives, water-rescue teams spend a frantic night pulling people from rooftops. Everyone is eventually accounted for, but it's a near thing, and the trauma runs deep.

Your models were right. The lesson you carry forward: good science isn't enough on its own — how clearly and forcefully it's communicated can be the difference between a warning heeded and a warning ignored.

sci_wait.title: The Window Closes
sci_wait.text:
You wait for firmer data. By the time the afternoon runs confirm the western surge threat, it's the evening before landfall and the roads are already clogging.

The mandatory evacuation goes out too late. Rain bands arrive ahead of schedule, highways flood, and thousands are trapped between home and safety when Wren comes ashore.

The science was eventually correct — but a forecast that arrives too late to act on is just a record of what went wrong. You'll spend a long time thinking about the hours you spent waiting for certainty that a storm would never give you.

farm_start.title: Two Days Out
farm_start.text:
The radio crackles with the hurricane warning as you finish the morning chores. Wren is coming, and Port Haven is in the cone. You've got 200 acres, a barn full of equipment, a nearly-ripe crop, and 60 head of cattle in the low pasture by the river.

You can't save everything. Where do you start?

choices.text: Move the cattle out of the low pasture to higher ground inland right away.
Race to harvest as much of the crop as you can before the rain hits.

farm_cattle.title: The Herd Comes First
farm_cattle.text:
You spend the better part of a day moving the herd to a leased pasture on high ground ten miles inland. It's exhausting, and it costs you the time you might have used on the crop — but the cattle are your livelihood, and the river pasture is exactly where the flooding will be worst.

With the animals safe, you turn back to the farmstead. There's still a day before the worst of it.

choices.text: Secure the equipment, board up the barn, then evacuate with your family.
Make one last run to haul the irrigation pumps off the floodplain before you go.

farm_wind_roll.title: Compounding Risk: The Squall Line
farm_wind_roll.text:
The irrigation pumps are worth a year's profit, and they're sitting right in the floodplain. You could make one fast run to haul them out before you evacuate.

But the leading edge of Wren is throwing off squall lines — sudden walls of wind and rain that can drop a flash flood on the low ground with almost no warning. If one hits while you're down there, you'll be caught in the worst possible place. Roll to see what the sky does.

roll.prompt: Click the die. If it lands on a 2 or a 4, a squall line hits while you're on the floodplain.
roll.goodText: The sky holds. You haul the pumps up to the ridge and get clear before the next band rolls in — a year's profit saved.
roll.badText: A squall line slams in out of nowhere. Wind flattens the reeds and a wall of flash-flood water comes down the channel toward you while you're still loading the trailer.

farm_pumps_saved.title: Pumps on the Ridge
farm_pumps_saved.text: The pumps are safe and the truck is loaded. You've bought back a season's income. Now there's just the question of you and the farmstead, with the worst of the storm still hours out.

choices.text: Take the win — load the family and evacuate to high ground.
Push your luck and stay to guard the place through the storm.

farm_pumps_caught.title: Caught in the Open
farm_pumps_caught.text: The water is rising over your boots and the wind is tearing at the trailer. The pumps are half-loaded. Every second you spend on them is a second the flood gets between you and the road home.

choices.text: Leave the pumps. Get in the truck and run for high ground now.
You're so close — finish loading the pumps first.

farm_close_call.title: A Hard Lesson, Cheaply Bought
farm_close_call.text:
You abandon the pumps and gun the truck up the rising lane, water spraying from the wheels, and break onto high ground just as the floodplain disappears behind you.

The pumps are gone — a brutal loss. But you're standing here to feel it, and so is your family. Some gambles you only get to make once. You won't bet your life on a piece of equipment again.

farm_harvest.title: Beating the Rain
farm_harvest.text:
You throw everything into harvesting. By dusk you've salvaged maybe a third of the crop — real money in the bank. But the sky to the south has turned an ugly green-grey, and the river is already rising faster than you've ever seen.

The cattle are still down in the low pasture, and the radio says the roads inland will flood by morning.

choices.text: Drop everything and move the cattle now, before the roads go under.
There's no time to move them safely — shelter in place with the herd and hope.

farm_secure.title: Battened Down
farm_secure.text:
You board the barn, chain the equipment to anchor points, and pull the truck and tractor up onto the ridge. Then you load the family and drive inland to the same high ground as the herd.

Wren is brutal. The river swallows the low pasture and laps at the farmhouse porch. But when the water recedes, the barn is standing, the equipment is muddy but intact, and all 60 head of cattle are alive.

You lost most of the crop and a season's income — but a farm is its land, its animals, and the people who work it. You still have all three. You'll rebuild.

farm_cattle_late.title: A Race Against the Water
farm_cattle_late.text:
You drive the herd toward high ground in the dark as the rain comes in sideways. The lead road is already ankle-deep and rising. You make it through — but not with everyone. A dozen head are lost to the flooding river, and the trailer nearly goes with them.

The surviving cattle and your family reach safety, soaked and shaken. You saved the harvest money and most of the herd, but the late start cost you animals you didn't have to lose.

Next season, you promise yourself, you'll move the herd the moment the warning comes — and let the crop take its chances.

farm_stay.title: Riding It Out
farm_stay.text:
You decide to stay. By midnight the river has jumped its banks and there's two feet of water in the yard. By dawn the low pasture is a lake, the cattle are scattering or drowning, and the water is still rising around the house.

You spend the worst night of your life on the roof of the barn, flashlight pointed at the sky, until a county rescue boat finds you the next afternoon.

You survive — but barely, and the rescuers who came for you took on the storm's risk too. Property can be rebuilt and animals replaced. The hardest lesson of Hurricane Wren is that nothing on the farm was worth staying for.

sci_start_comm.title: The Forecast Lands (You're Not Alone)
sci_start_comm.text:
It's 6 a.m. and Hurricane Wren is intensifying. The forecast still shows a wide landfall window across Port Haven.

This year is different: a regional climate-resilience coalition is active, with volunteer response teams, neighboring-county emergency managers on a shared call, and a trusted community radio network ready to amplify whatever you send. You don't have to carry the warning alone.

choices.text: Recommend a mandatory evacuation now — the coalition already has buses, shelters, and volunteers staged.
First check the compounding upstream-rain risk, with the coalition's hydrologists helping you model it.

sci_compound_roll_comm.title: Compounding Risk: The Stalled Rain Band
sci_compound_roll_comm.text:
The same threat the base scenario hides: a slow rain band may stall over the upstream watershed and stack river flooding onto the surge. This time you're not modeling it alone — the coalition's hydrologists are running parallel forecasts and the community radio is standing by to push whatever you decide.

It still comes down to whether the band stalls. Roll to see.

roll.prompt: Click the die. If it lands on a 2 or a 4, the rain band stalls and the floods compound.
roll.goodText: The band drifts out to sea. With the coalition's hydrologists confirming it, you issue a clean, confident surge warning and the community network carries it everywhere.
roll.badText: The band stalls — but because the coalition was watching the rivers too, you catch the compound flood the moment the gauges spike.

sci_compound_hit_comm.title: Two Floods at Once — Together
sci_compound_hit_comm.text: River gauges upstream are spiking while the surge builds offshore. The combined flood will reach neighborhoods nobody planned to evacuate. But the coalition has a pre-built expanded-evacuation plan on the shelf, and the radio network can reach those neighborhoods in minutes.

choices.text: Trigger the coalition's expanded-evacuation plan and let the community network spread the word.
Bypass the coalition and run it up the official chain alone to keep it 'clean'.

sci_evac_comm.title: A Warning That Carries
sci_evac_comm.text:
The evacuation order goes out — and this time it doesn't just go out, it lands. Community radio, volunteer canvassers, and neighboring-county crews move people who would never have heard a top-down alert in time. Shelters are staffed and open before the first rain band.

When the 14-foot surge floods the western zones, the streets are empty and the shelters are full. The science was the same as always. What changed is that a community was ready to act on it the moment you spoke.

sci_evac_comm_big.title: Ahead of Both Floods, Together
sci_evac_comm_big.text:
You trigger the coalition's expanded plan. Within the hour, volunteers and neighboring crews are clearing the entire combined flood footprint while community radio explains, calmly and in three languages, exactly where the water will go.

The river and the sea arrive together and take streets no prior plan had ever flagged — but they take no one. The after-action report has a single headline: the compounding flood was survivable because the warning and the people to act on it were already wired together before the storm.

sci_start_pro.title: Before the Season: Build Resilience
sci_start_pro.text:
It's months before hurricane season. You have the budget and political capital for exactly one major resilience investment. Whatever you build now is what you'll have to work with when the next big storm comes.

Choose your investment.

choices.text: Fund a dense real-time storm-surge sensor and high-resolution modeling network.
Establish a pre-approved, automatic evacuation-trigger framework with local officials.

sci_pro_sensors.title: The Storm Arrives — and You Can See It
sci_pro_sensors.text: Wren forms, and this time your sensor network and high-res models pin the western surge with high confidence three days out. There is no uncertainty to hide behind, for you or for the officials. The forecast is unambiguous and early.

choices.text: Issue the early, confident mandatory evacuation while there's plenty of time.
Even with rock-solid data, wait for political consensus before recommending anything.

sci_pro_triggers.title: The Storm Arrives — and the Rules Are Set
sci_pro_triggers.text:
Wren forms, and the framework you built months ago is already humming: if modeled surge crosses an agreed threshold, a mandatory evacuation fires automatically, no debate, no political flinching.

The surge forecast climbs toward the threshold.

choices.text: Let the automatic trigger run exactly as designed.
Override the trigger and hold for consensus 'just to be safe'.

sci_compound_roll_pro.title: Compounding Risk: The Stalled Rain Band
sci_compound_roll_pro.text:
The trigger has fired and the western zones are clearing. The one thing your framework can't control is the upstream watershed: a rain band may stall and stack river flooding onto the surge.

But you designed the framework to widen automatically if a second threshold trips. Roll to see whether the band stalls.

roll.prompt: Click the die. If it lands on a 2 or a 4, the rain band stalls and the floods compound.
roll.goodText: The band moves out to sea. The single-threshold evacuation was exactly right, and it happened automatically and early.
roll.badText: The band stalls — but the river gauges trip your second threshold, and the framework expands the evacuation on its own, before anyone has to argue about it.

sci_evac_pro.title: The Storm You Were Ready For
sci_evac_pro.text:
The evacuation happened early, calmly, and without a single hour lost to doubt — because the hard decisions were made months ago, when the sky was clear and there was time to think.

Wren floods the western zones on schedule and finds them empty. The lesson of the proactive path is quiet but profound: the most lives are saved not in the frantic 48 hours before landfall, but in the unglamorous season before, when someone chose to build the system that would act when it mattered.

sci_evac_pro_compound.title: The Framework Holds
sci_evac_pro_compound.text:
The compounding flood — the disaster that overwhelmed the base scenario — barely registers as a crisis here. Your framework saw the second threshold trip and widened the evacuation automatically, hours before the rivers and the surge met in the streets.

Homes are lost. No one is. You spend the storm not fighting for a last-minute warning, but watching a system you built do exactly what you designed it to do. That is what resilience looks like when it works.

farm_start_comm.title: Two Days Out (Neighbors Calling)
farm_start_comm.text: The hurricane warning hits as you finish chores — but so does your phone. The valley's farmers run a storm phone tree, and the co-op is already mobilizing shared trailers and spare hands. You've got 200 acres, a barn of equipment, a nearly-ripe crop, and 60 head of cattle in the low river pasture. This time, you don't have to face it alone.

choices.text: Take the co-op's extra trailers and move the whole herd to high ground fast.
Split the help — neighbors harvest while you and a crew start on the cattle.

farm_cattle_comm.title: The Herd Comes First — With Help
farm_cattle_comm.text: With three borrowed trailers and four extra pairs of hands, the herd is on high ground inland by early afternoon — a job that took you a full exhausting day alone. The cattle are safe, and for once you have time to spare before the storm.

choices.text: Use the saved time to secure the equipment and evacuate as a convoy with the neighbors.
Make a run for the floodplain pumps — and this time a neighbor rides along in a second truck.

farm_split_comm.title: Many Hands
farm_split_comm.text: The phone tree pays off. While one crew runs cattle to high ground, another brings in a real chunk of the crop — money you'd have lost entirely on your own. By dusk the herd is safe and a third of the harvest is in the barn.

choices.text: Quit while you're ahead — convoy out to high ground with the neighbors.
One last pump run on the floodplain, with a neighbor following in a second truck.

farm_wind_roll_comm.title: Compounding Risk: The Squall Line
farm_wind_roll_comm.text:
The irrigation pumps are worth a year's profit, sitting in the floodplain. With a neighbor following in a second truck, you make a run for them — but Wren's leading edge is throwing off squall lines that can drop a flash flood on the low ground with no warning.

The difference this time: if it goes bad, you're not down there alone. Roll to see what the sky does.

roll.prompt: Click the die. If it lands on a 2 or a 4, a squall line hits while you're on the floodplain.
roll.goodText: The sky holds. Two trucks haul the pumps out in half the time, and you're both clear before the next band — a year's profit saved, together.
roll.badText: A squall line slams in. Flash water comes down the channel — but your neighbor's truck is right there, engine running, headlights cutting the rain.

farm_pumps_caught_comm.title: Caught — But Not Alone
farm_pumps_caught_comm.text: The water is rising fast and the wind is tearing at the trailers. The pumps are half-loaded. Your neighbor is already waving you toward the high road, their truck idling on the last patch of solid ground.

choices.text: Leave the pumps. Jump in and follow your neighbor out.
Wave them off and try to finish loading the pumps yourself.

farm_secure_comm.title: Out Together, Whole
farm_secure_comm.text:
The convoy rolls out to high ground in the last clear hour — your family, your neighbors, the herd, and a barn's worth of equipment chained down and battened behind you. Wren floods the low pasture and laps at the porches, but the valley's farms emptied out as one.

When the water drops, you'll spend weeks helping each other muck out barns and chase down strays. You lost some crop and some sleep. You kept everything that couldn't be replaced — and you learned that a flood is a lot smaller when a whole valley faces it shoulder to shoulder.

farm_close_call_comm.title: A Loss You Walked Away From
farm_close_call_comm.text:
You leave the pumps and follow your neighbor's taillights up the rising lane, both trucks breaking onto high ground as the floodplain vanishes behind you.

The pumps are gone — a real loss. But you're standing in the rain next to the person who came back for you, and you'll do the same for them next season. Some things you can't replace, and some of them aren't equipment. You'll buy new pumps. You can't buy what made your neighbor turn that truck around.

farm_start_pro.title: Before the Season: Build Resilience
farm_start_pro.text:
It's the quiet season, months before any storm. You've set aside money and time for one major investment to make the farm more resilient. Whatever you build now is what will be standing — or not — when the next hurricane comes up the coast.

Choose your investment.

choices.text: Build an elevated livestock refuge mound with proper drainage on the high pasture.
Invest in a mobile pump trailer and pre-arrange an inland pasture lease with a scouted route.

farm_pro_mound.title: The Storm Arrives — and the Herd Knows Where to Go
farm_pro_mound.text: Wren is two days out. There's no frantic dawn-to-dusk drive this time: you open one gate and the cattle walk themselves up onto the engineered refuge mound, high and dry above any flood the river has ever managed. The hardest, slowest job of the base scenario simply doesn't exist anymore.

choices.text: Secure the equipment and evacuate your family calmly — the herd is already safe.
Stay on the property to keep an eye on the herd through the storm.

farm_pro_lease.title: The Storm Arrives — and You Have a Plan
farm_pro_lease.text: Wren is two days out, and everything you'd normally scramble for is already arranged: the pumps live on a mobile trailer, the inland pasture is leased and waiting, and you scouted both the main route and a backup weeks ago.

choices.text: Hitch up and head out early on your pre-planned inland route, herd and pumps together.
Wait until the last minute to leave — no sense going early.

farm_route_roll_pro.title: Compounding Risk: The Bridge
farm_route_roll_pro.text:
You leave early, herd and pumps in tow. The one thing your planning couldn't fully control is the low bridge on the main route — in a fast-rising flood it can wash out with little warning.

But you didn't plan just one route. Roll to see whether the bridge holds.

roll.prompt: Click the die. If it lands on a 2 or a 4, the bridge washes out before you reach it.
roll.goodText: The bridge holds. You cross with hours to spare and reach the leased pasture with the whole herd, the pumps, and your family intact.
roll.badText: Word comes over the radio: the low bridge is already underwater. The main route is gone — but you scouted a backup for exactly this.

farm_route_caught_pro.title: The Backup Route
farm_route_caught_pro.text: The main bridge is out and floodwater is climbing toward the lane. The decision in front of you is the one your planning was meant to make easy.

choices.text: Turn onto the backup route you scouted weeks ago.
Risk it and try to ford the washed-out bridge to save time.

farm_secure_pro.title: The Storm You Prepared For
farm_secure_pro.text:
You evacuate in daylight, unhurried, with the herd already safe and the equipment secured. Wren does its worst to the low ground — and finds nothing of yours there to take.

When you come back, you muck out, you reset, and within a season the farm is whole. The work that saved you wasn't done in the storm. It was done months earlier, on an ordinary clear day, when you chose to build for the flood instead of hoping it wouldn't come.

farm_secure_pro_alt.title: The Road You Already Knew
farm_secure_pro_alt.text:
You turn onto the backup route without slowing down, because you've driven it before for exactly this moment. It's longer, but it's high and dry, and it carries you, the herd, and the pumps to the leased pasture as the storm closes in behind you.

The main bridge is gone; it doesn't matter. The difference between a disaster and an inconvenience, you decide, is often just a second plan made before you needed it.
